body:

Grounded Investment Company (GIC), a Dutch impact investment fund, managed by Grounded, that backs African food processors, has reached €12 million in commitments. The Livelihood Impact Fund (LIF) is the lead investor, with Ecosia, VP Capital and CarbonFix also participating, alongside existing investor DOEN Participaties and a number of family offices and individual investors.

The fund has a target of up to €50 million. A first close of €17–20 million is planned for mid-2027, with a final close in mid-2029.

GIC invests in African processors that buy from smallholder farmers, focusing on high-value crops that store well, including coffee, spices, nuts, cocoa and tea.

Beyond capital, GIC provides in-house regenerative agronomy support through soil and regenerative-farming specialists, field officers and a research farm in Zambia, along with a multi-year roadmap that supports farmers towards organic certification. Market access comes through Grounded Ingredients, the trading company of fund manager Grounded, which prepays part of a processor’s contracted harvest, tests quality before shipment and sells to European buyers. The trading company is set to be brought into the fund.

Thekla Teunis, managing partner at GIC, said: “Regenerative agriculture doesn’t need a subsidy to compete. When a well-run processor brings regenerative methods to its farmers, yields and quality go up, input costs go down and farmers earn more. Among a group of coffee farmers we monitor in Uganda, the typical farmer lifted cherry yields by around a third in a single year after adopting on-farm compost and bio-fertiliser – and several more than doubled their harvest. This close lets us take that model to many more processors, and we are grateful to the Livelihood Impact Fund, Ecosia, VP Capital, CarbonFix and all our investors for backing it.”

GIC takes significant stakes and builds the business alongside founders, rather than spreading many small bets. First investments range from €300,000 to €750,000 per company, with follow-ons of up to €2–3 million. Around 70% of the fund is reserved for follow-on investment in the companies that perform.

Gijs Boers, also a managing partner at GIC, added: “Africa’s economy has a few large companies and very many small ones; the mid-sized firms are missing. We start with modest tickets, stay for the long term and put our capital and time behind the companies that perform. With most of our team based in Kenya and South Africa, we are building the regional processing groups the continent needs.”

The fund has a life of up to 13 years and is classified as an Article 9 fund – the EU’s strictest sustainability category – under the Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation.

The current portfolio includes speciality coffee company Zombo Coffee Partners in Uganda, organic spice business Trianon Spices and cashew company Mama Cashew in Tanzania, and spice company Dynamic Intertrade in South Africa.

Jan-Maarten Mulder, senior advisor at LIF, commented: “Agricultural processing companies are a key lever for improving rural livelihoods in Africa. By investing in strong local processors, Grounded will help thousands of smallholder farmers access better markets, receive higher prices for their crops and be rewarded for adopting regenerative farming practices. This ability to create lasting impact for farmers by building commercially sustainable businesses is why LIF is pleased to lead this investment round.”

Pieter van Midwoud, chief tree officer at Ecosia, a Berlin-based search engine that dedicates its profits to climate action, noted: “Agroforestry systems, that combine trees with other crops, are key for a resilient and profitable farm, even more so in places that are vulnerable to the effects of climate change. GIC puts agroforestry at the centre of how African export crops are grown – coffee, spices and nuts cultivated among trees, with farmers making their own natural fertilisers instead of buying chemicals. This way, GIC stimulates the planting and growing of millions of trees in their supply chains, exactly the sort of systemic change that our planet needs and that Ecosia is after.”

Jarno van den Heuvel, investment director at climate investment platform CarbonFix, remarked: “Regenerative farming in Africa is a deeply neglected climate pathway, and GIC’s model has the potential to be truly transformational. Those are exactly the levers we look for to catalyse impact where mainstream capital isn’t flowing yet.”

Thijn van Doorne, senior manager funds at VP Capital, a single family office based in Belgium and the Netherlands, said: “We look for investments that combine sound business fundamentals with lasting impact. We do believe that GIC, through their repeatable value creation playbook, is able to build profitable stable processors improving the African agri-ecosystem both from an impact and financial point of view.”
